rich_summary: At dawn the royal palace follows its daily ritual: bards, musicians, brahmins, and attendants gather to awaken the king with praises, music, and ceremony. Servants prepare perfumes, oils, and golden vessels for the king’s morning ablutions while the entire court waits for him to rise. When he does not appear, the women of the palace attempt to wake him. Touching his body, they realize with growing dread that he shows no sign of life. Their fear turns to certainty: the king has died during the night. The palace, once filled with praise and music, becomes a place of shock and grief. Queen Kaushalya and Queen Sumitra, already broken by the exile of their sons, lie overwhelmed by sorrow, their faded splendor compared to stars hidden behind clouds. The scene marks the tragic consequence of Rama’s exile and the collapse of royal order in Ayodhya.

The pivotal moment when attendants realize the king is dead, turning the ceremonial morning into tragedy.

The poetic comparison of the grieving queens to stars hidden by clouds underscores the dimming of royal glory and hope.

top_scenes.scene_text: At dawn the palace courtyard fills with bards, brahmins, musicians, birds, and attendants singing and playing instruments while the golden palace awaits the king’s awakening.
Royal attendants gently try to awaken the king in his chamber, then recoil in shock as they realize his body is lifeless.
Queen Kaushalya and Queen Sumitra lie pale and grief-stricken in the dim palace chamber, their sorrow likened to stars hidden behind dark clouds.
